title: Analyses of the prevalence distribution of tularaemia (Francisella tularensis) in different vectors and the seroprevalence of the local population within an epidemiological high-prevalence cluster at Tuniberg/Kaiserstuhl
summary:
Tularemia (hare plague), caused by the bacterium Francisella tularensis, is a potentially serious infectious disease that is notifiable under the IfSG and is transmitted by certain insects (vectors, e.g. ticks) and can affect animals and humans. In recent years, increasing numbers of human cases of Francisella tularensis have been observed in various regions of Germany. This is currently attributed to increased tick activity. Based on the clinical cases, a local accumulation of diseases was observed in the Tuniberg/Kaiserstuhl area. In this project, we would therefore like to investigate how frequently Francisella tularensis occurs in the environment (e.g. ticks, mosquitoes, soil and water) within an area where transmission is suspected. In addition, studies are to be carried out on the general spread of the disease in the population of a region with a high incidence of the disease (Tuniberg/Kaiserstuhl area) and the population outside the area. 
For this purpose, ticks, mosquitoes and environmental samples from the defined area will be systematically collected and analysed for the presence of the pathogen. At the same time, voluntary blood donors in the Breisgau-Hochschwarzwald district will be tested to determine whether antibodies against F. tularensis are present in their blood - i.e. whether the person has already had contact with the pathogen. The samples come from the regular blood donation; only an additional small serum sample is analysed. In the event of a positive result in the blood sample, the participating person will be contacted again to determine the exact possible site of infection and to clarify whether further medical examination or treatment is required, subject to their consent. In addition, confirmed cases must be reported to the responsible health authorities as part of the statutory reporting obligation. 
Further analyses are carried out to determine whether the same vector samples also contain evidence of other tick- or mosquito-borne pathogens (e.g. TBE, West Nile virus, Borrelia). The remaining blood samples are stored and possibly kept for later tests for these other pathogens. The aim is to identify possible regional ‘infection hotspots’, to be able to better assess the risk and to contribute to the long-term health protection of the population.
